en: Preface to the *Kejiao guan cuoyao lun* (Abridged Treatise on the Essentials of Teaching and Contemplation):
Although the complete text of the *Kejiao guan cuoyao lun* has not been seen, its author and the number of fascicles remain unknown.

However, at the end of its fourth fascicle, it states: "The 'Discourse on the Three Thousand [Realms]' by the late master Wankong Heshang is appended herein. Thus, it was composed by one of his disciples.
It is certain that the scroll ends at the fourth fascicle. My teacher once borrowed this book at the Xingsheng Chan Monastery in Chang’an and transcribed it there, whereupon he sighed, saying:
“Alas, this book contains so many profound expositions, yet it has been lost and remains incomplete. The other day he commanded me, saying:
‘This is like a single piece of jade from Mount Kunlun; how could one bear to discard it? Why not have it printed and circulated? (I) [acted accordingly].
Thereupon, I have appended this preface in the vernacular for the sake of future scribes; it is my hope that readers may obtain a complete copy of this work and supplement it accordingly.
Written on the first day of winter in the first year of the Hōei era by the śrāmaṇera Kakudai of the Anraku Hermitage on Mount Tiantai.

To seek Prajñā is for the emotions to be stirred within; because the three requests and the oral seeking of the spiritual capacity must coexist, the subsequent [stages] necessarily follow.
Furthermore, based on what has been discussed previously, there are distinctions between the intimate and the distant; this is the general outline.

From antiquity, when discussing the mouth, its magnitude, its basis, and its existence or non-existence, and so forth—a detailed examination of the texts in the commentaries reveals nothing that should be doubted.

As it is said: "The mechanism (*jī*) is real while the sentiment (*qíng*) is provisional; the sentiment is real while the mouth is provisional. Moreover, the mechanism resides in the Mahāyāna, while the sentiment seeks the reality of the past.
If one seeks the Mahāyāna with the heart while asking about past realities with the mouth, and if this is indeed the case, then the capacity (*indriya*) is great while the expression is small;
the heart penetrates both the Great and the Small Vehicles, as is clearly evident in the text—so why should there be any doubt? Someone may say:

"At the moment of seeking with the mouth, although the heart and intention are set upon the Great [Vehicle], what can be done about the text of the 'three requests,' which contains such phrases as 'I wish for you to preach the foremost Dharma' and 'I desire to hear the complete Path'?"
One might ask: "Is it permissible to call this 'seeking'? I reply: One should know that at the time of the three requests, the capacity for the Mahāyāna was activated;
the yearning for the milk of the Dharma was even greater than during the time of the two ghees.

However, because [the Buddha] heard only a brief opening and rejection as a skillful means, the mind that had previously clung to the truth and preserved the fruit suddenly fell into self-disarray. Thus, within the realm of emotion, one could not avoid hesitation; hence it is called the "cart."
Because he rejected expedient means and lost the reality, it was necessary to seek this [truth].

As for his verbal requests, although there were words such as "I wish you would preach the foremost Dharma" and "I desire to hear the complete path," these were merely seeking in accordance with the Buddha’s own words;
since those words did not primarily concern the Mahāyāna, they are called "small. What is meant by "in accordance with the Buddha’s own words" refers to the brief opening [of the teaching].
The text states that the Buddha has accomplished a most rare and difficult-to-understand Dharma; it further says that he is "fully endowed with the practice of all paths.
Upon hearing this critique of expedient means, Śāriputra doubted whether his own realization was truly real, and thus he repeated the Buddha’s words several times to extend his request.
Yet, he still did not know what the "first and fully endowed path" actually was. My Patriarch said:
If one seeks the truth of what was said in the past, one will know that the question lies merely in the minor details. Someone may ask:
"Since the aspiration for the Buddha-way is already the movement of a Mahāyāna capacity, how can it be considered a mere verbal pursuit, like seeking the root through a metaphor? I reply:
One who attains the great path does not follow narrow byways; one who clarifies the great meaning is not constrained by fragmentary texts—this is the teaching of our Patriarch.
The verses following the chapter on Śākyamuni serve as the basis for the subsequent parables; they clarify only their general meaning.
If there are one or two names that do not correspond [to those in the parable], one must necessarily interpret them according to their underlying sense so as not to obstruct the intent of the text.
For example, "peace and security" is taken as the basis for the "insecurity of the three realms" below, and "various dharma-gates" is taken as the basis for what follows.
There is one section that serves as the basis for this analogy; it is not singular, so please examine it in detail, and you will naturally be able to clarify its great significance.
How could it be limited to the single passage concerning the seeking of the carriage?
Discourse on the King of Sutras of All Schools:
Now, what is called the "King of Sutras" is the Middle Way. For the Middle possesses the power of universal integration;

it is sovereign over all teachings, being both honored and ultimate, and thus receives the title of "King. Therefore, it is said that among the various sutras, there are those whose meaning refers to the Dharmakāya.

It is precisely because it is called the "King of Sutras" that it is so designated; otherwise, were one to merely obtain this sutra without [the context of] the path of teaching, it would not be called a "king.
If this were the case, why does the text state: "Among all gradual and sudden sutras, there is none that is not called the King of Sutras regarding the point it elucidates"?
Furthermore, it says: "Since the teachings are divided into Great and Small, the kings are likewise distinguished by honor and status," and even: "The Teacher of Expedient Means..."
The king is named "Not Non-existent" (*Anabhibhūta*); thus, both the principle of partial truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*) and the three previous provisional fruits may all be called "kings.
What is the meaning of this? Because from of old they have not understood the intent of the text, it has been said that the "King of Sūtras" encompasses both the present and the future;

consequently, there have been various disputes regarding whether [the title] applies or not. If one says that for a sūtra to be the "King of Sūtras," it must be discussed in terms of encompassing both the present and the future, then as for the sūtra...
The essence must also be discussed, for the essence of the King [of Sutras] is likewise the Middle Way. Examining it by this standard, one knows that the old explanations are circuitous.
One should know that the "King of Sutras" takes only the Perfect Middle as its basis; because it is sovereign over all other sutras, it receives the name "King.
In the past, the Perfect Middle was sovereign only within the various sutras of its own section; however, when it comes to preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, [it is sovereign over all].

Yuan then said: "Now, regarding what I shall now explain concerning the sovereign mastery throughout the entire dispensation (*ekayāna*), if it is clarified in this manner alone, it will be concise and easy to understand, and there will be no divergence from the essence of the sutra.
Question: "How is it that the text of the *Shuji* (Commentary) so clearly encompasses both the provisional and the gradual teachings?
Answer: "Each passage has its own specific intent; they cannot be viewed according to a single standard. Indeed, as for the text..."

Regarding the phrase "the assembly of kings," if one does not distinguish between the partial and the perfect, the gradual and the sudden, as well as the provisional and the ultimate, all of which may be termed "kings," then how can the meaning of "assembly" be perceived?

Consequently, there arose various schools with differing views, some asserting that each individual is called a "king" and that being "foremost" constitutes the state of kingship; others further claimed that this sūtra harmonizes and integrates these positions.
In various teachings and the like, this is an explanation of the phrase "the assembly of kings" based on the *nikāyas* (sections) and the *dharmas* (teachings).
One should know that this is merely an exegesis applied to the specific passage at hand; it is by no means an exposition on the general course of the *Mahāsāṃghika* school.

From antiquity, those who did not understand this have indiscriminately collected [these texts] because their names are identical, which is incorrect. Later generations, moreover, because they had already been collected, [continued this practice].

To discuss this while conflating it with the Great Path (Dàtú) is likewise incorrect; yet, the purport of the Great Path takes only the "circle within the circle" as its sovereign principle, wherein the meanings of pervasion and limitation, separation and union, are all contained therein.
This is as clear as the midday sun in the *Sijiaoji* (Record of the Four Teachings), so there is no need for further prolixity.

Regarding the title *King of Sūtras* (*Sūtrarāja*) appearing prominently in this scripture alone among the *Luminous Sūtras* (*Prabhāsa-sūtra*), it is because this scripture encompasses the four teachings;

since it possesses both the nature of a sūtra and the further meaning of being a "king" that governs and subsumes them, the name of "sovereign" (*svatantra*) is established. Therefore, it is called a "text."

The title "King of Sutras" indicates that it encompasses all scriptures; however, if one were to discuss this solely from the perspective of its own specific division (*nikāya*), its comprehensive inclusion would be limited to the various teachings within that division alone.
Yet, when my ancestor, the Imperial Preceptor Huiwang, discussed comprehensive inclusion in his writings, he did so by means of three meanings.
First, it universally encompasses all dharma-gates, beginning from the Three Paths and ending with the Three Virtues, whether they be delusions or...
Whether they be obstacles to wisdom or its virtues, none fail to be subsumed within this sutra.

Next, it universally subsumes all scriptural teachings, from the *Avataṃsaka* at their beginning to the *Nirvāṇa* at their end; whether gradual or sudden, partial or perfect, none fail to be subsumed within this sutra.
Finally, it universally subsumes all stages of perfection, from the fundamental nature of reality (*li-xing*) at their beginning to—
Ultimately, whether it be delusion or awakening, partiality or fulfillment, there is nothing that is not subsumed within this sutra.
Since it subsumes all dharma-gates, all scriptural teachings, and all stages of perfection,

one should know that to speak exclusively of the Vaipulya [Prajñāpāramitā] as being incapable of expressing this is to anticipate the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and speak by leaping over the intervening stages.
"After the Master’s passing, if one explains the sutras without relying on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, how could one possibly exhaust the meaning of the entire lifetime of his teaching?
This is the firm dictum of our Patriarch. If one understands this principle, then the doctrines of the three mundane, the three true, and the three middle [truths] will find their proper destination.

Siming specifically elaborated upon these by means of the sevenfold two-truths, desiring to profoundly exhaust the source of transformation throughout the Master’s lifetime and to clarify the sutras after his passing."
This is because they follow the same standard track. Does the *Wen* not say: "In this way, the elucidation of the scriptures is gathered within a single transformation, leaving nothing unexhausted"?

Now, if one wishes to gather [all teachings] within a single transformation, what could be proposed other than the seven and two truths? For these seven and two truths have both partial and complete aspects, as well as direct and accommodated aspects;
it is not only that the meaning of the scriptures can be clarified by them, but they are also the very essence of this King [of Sutras].

The underlying meaning can also be clarified; thus, we know that the teachings of the Four Clarifiers (Sijiaming) are not to be lightly disparaged. Have you not seen the text of Tiantai, which states:
"However, the King of Sutras is one, yet as it establishes teachings according to conditions, its names differ.

From the *Avataṃsaka* being named the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) to the *Nirvāṇa* being called the Teacher of Buddhas, these are all different names for the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), serving as a common basis for all sutras."
If one examines this text, it becomes even more evident that the explanations of the Four Ming Masters are most worthy of trust.
The various masters of Gushan, Fushishi, and Jingjue each interpreted [the teachings] according to their own individual opinions;

not only were they unable to encompass the entirety of the Buddha’s transformation, but they also left omissions and errors regarding the four teachings within the specific sections. Since their strengths and weaknesses are already established, it may well be set aside without further discussion.

Since ancient times, it has been commonly transmitted that the Indian Master of Repentance (Chánzhǔ) held the view that "the three conventional [truths] destroy the ancients" and "the three ultimates eliminate the king.
These claims appear plausible and are easily able to delude people; therefore, one cannot help but debate and clarify them. Furthermore, his words state:

"The three conventional [truths] are the conventionalities of the partial teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Nirvāṇa*; the three ultimates are the ultimates of the three partial teachings; and the 'three in the middle' are the three [truths] themselves."

To correlate the three divisions of the Perfect Teaching with the inconceivable True and the Conventional in this manner may be a skillful way of harmonizing the commentary (*śāstra*), yet it does not avoid being confused regarding the great purport.

Why is this? The commentary’s discussion of the three conventional, three true, and three middle [realms] primarily elucidates the *Sūtra of Radiant Light* as the King of Sutras, while simultaneously encompassing all the scriptures of the entire dispensation.
How can one then divide these into three specific sections? Furthermore, this would conversely imply that the *Sūtra of Radiant Light* is not the King of Sutras. Is this not so?
This is acceptable. Since the *Avataṃsaka* is called the "Dharmakāya," the *Vaipulya* the "True Aspect" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*),

the *Prajñāpāramitā* the "Mother of Buddhas," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* the "Crest Jewel," and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* the "Teacher of Buddhas"— all of which are alternative names for the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) that universally serve as the essence of all sūtras—
then how could it be that what is taught throughout the five periods of teaching is not all alternative names for the Dharma-nature, and thus universally qualify as the sovereign?
Can one point exclusively to the three divisions [of the Esoteric teachings] as the ultimate refuge?
Not only does this reveal that one's own division is not the "King," but it also reveals that the *Lotus Sūtra* is not the "King of all sūtras"—this is doubly untenable.

Furthermore, when our Patriarch confronted and refuted the Tripitaka Master Zhenti, he used the three dharmas of perfect fusion to dismantle those three dharmas of partial correspondence to the three sūtras, stating: "If one advances, one does not achieve the Perfect; if one retreats, one does not achieve the Separate."

Furthermore, when has anyone ever refuted the Four Teachings by means of the ultimate and conventional truths? This point has already been clarified in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) through its refutations and establishments as clearly as the sun and stars;
why then must one further subject it here to additional refutation?

Thirdly, since the refutation of the ancient interpretation that "eliminates the King" is incorrect, the discourse on the sevenfold two-truths can be naturally trusted, and the meaning of the recorded text is thereby explained.
The path to clarity does not depend on further elaboration; its meaning is already manifest and radiant. For now, I shall briefly provide an explanation:
one should take the texts of the various scriptures as the basis for instruction and rely upon them, using the principles for interpreting the sutras as the standard.

By correlating the various synonymous terms for the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) and contemplating deeply how they are subsumed within the discourse of a single transformation, one will come to understand the seven [aspects].
The interpretation of the two truths is not a matter of mere whim. If that is so, is it then the case that Ciyun (Zhiyuan) is insufficient as a model?
Or have I perhaps examined this: all of Ciyun’s writings from his lifetime are recorded in the *Tianzhu jinyuan ji* and other collections;
if the doctrine of "destroying the old and eliminating the king" had truly originated with Ciyun, why would it alone not be included therein? It is just like Ciyun himself regarding...
In the "Chapter on the Essential Nature of Radiance," I have a slight doubt and thus inquire in a five-character verse:
Why did you, O Siming, not seek clarification regarding this particular major point where there appears to be a discrepancy?

Furthermore, since Siming and Ciyun were fellow students under Baoyun, and Baoyun frequently lectured on these profound passages, Siming and Ciyun must certainly have received his oral instructions face-to-face.
"How could the compassionate teachings be the same as those of the student, yet the views suddenly become so discordant?
Inferring from this, it is clear that such a doctrine did not originate with Ciyun.
It must have been the work of someone fond of novelty who wished to exploit Ciyun’s great reputation to advance their own arguments."
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* is cited to clarify the passage concerning the "reception and integration" (*bei jie*).
This text was composed by the Master of Records (*Jizhu*), who weighed and deliberated upon the intent of the sūtra; its meaning is difficult to perceive. One should first ask:

regarding the thirty-six passages [of the sūtra], the commentary provides an extensive explanation, yet it never mentions "reception and integration. Upon what basis did the Master of Records claim that these were for the benefit of those with "sharp faculties"?

Question: Do the faculties (indriya) enter into the Separate (Bhedābhisamaya) or the Perfect (Samantabhadra) [teachings]? Answer: According to the sutras, the three vehicles equally contemplate the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
As the commentary on the *Śāstra* explains, this is like the three animals crossing a river—the depth of the water they reach represents the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Sāmānya-nirdeśa).

Regarding the conclusion of the benefits in the sutra, which mentions "the reality-mark (lakṣaṇa) in one lifetime" and "the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in two lifetimes," the commentary points out that these correspond to the "diminishing of births" (*huǎnshēng*) as taught in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The meaning is that this refers to the stage of destroying ignorance through the transformation of birth by means of reduction;

since this is a contemplation common to the three vehicles, if a Bodhisattva were to destroy the delusions of ignorance without being "received" [into the higher stage], this text could not be reconciled.

Furthermore, the commentary on the twenty-fifth section of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-parivarta*, concerning the fourfold differences in the wisdom that contemplates causes and conditions, states: "This is precisely the 'reception of the distinct [vehicle] into the common [path]."
The meaning extends to the explanation of the current text, which indicates that it is identical to that chapter, stating: "As in the initial teaching of the Lion’s Roar, one should know this.

Thus, both these passages are teachings for the sake of guiding ordinary beings; because their underlying intent is profound and obscure, the Master of the Record (Jizang) specifically relies on this point to provide his judgment and interpretation.
He further clarifies his intention, saying: "One need only observe the concluding assemblies of the various sutras to understand [this]."
The meaning of "common" and "distinct" as explained in the *Daode* (Treatise on the Way) lies precisely here. Once this meaning is grasped, the interpretation of the text is not difficult.

Furthermore, while the text clearly indicates thirty-six passages that collectively cite the three vehicles as equally contemplating the true reality (*dharmatā*), along with the concluding benefits and so forth, you have instead cited the passage from the *Siṃhanāda-parivarta* concerning the fourfold differences in the wisdom that contemplates dependent origination.

As for "textual variations," it is likely that although the names and phrases differ, their underlying meaning is not distinct; therefore, they may be used interchangeably. Why is this? That chapter states:
"The twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature, and Buddha-nature is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

This text, however, says: "This is named the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), named the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), named ultimate wisdom (*atyanta-jñāna*), and named the emptiness of the ultimate truth. Thus, [the meanings] correspond.
The commentary explains this passage by indicating that it is identical to the [preceding] chapter; thus we know that while the texts of the two chapters differ, their meaning is the same.

In that [preceding] chapter there are four wisdoms, whereas in the present text there are only three; this is likewise a difference in the method of expansion and contraction. That chapter expands the "superior wisdom" (*ūrdhva-jñāna*) into two wisdoms because it distinguishes between the Separate (*vyāvṛtta*) and the Perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) [teachings].
Since those abiding in the Separate [Vehicle] have not yet shattered ignorance, it is said that their vision is not fully clear (*avyakta*). The Perfect [Vehicle], however, is clear.

Because it has already been broken upon abiding [in that stage], it is said that "seeing is clear and distinct. The present text, however, speaks generally based on the stage where ignorance is destroyed, hence it mentions "one birth, two births," and so forth.

Yet, the Master of the *Ji* (the *Fahua wenju*) applies this analogy to the other [teachings] by dividing them into two categories of teaching; thus he says, "The true aspect (*dharmatā*) is the specific principle (*viśeṣa-naya*)," etc.

This is because, according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekadeśanā*), the Path of Realization (*darśana-mārga*) at the first stage (*bhūmi*) is identical to the second stage of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*).

Because there still remains a separation and no one to personally witness the practice, one lifetime is assigned to the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) and two lifetimes are assigned to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).
This is merely a distinction between the two teachings based on the principle of one or two lifetimes;

it is the single reality of the Dharma-realm of true thusness (shixiang fajie), and there was originally no other intent behind it. Thus, the figures of ten thousand and five thousand mentioned in the text seem to be inconsistent with—

The discrepancies in the scriptural texts arise because names and characteristics are inconsistent; there is no need to force an interpretation. According to the commentary (*shu*), "one birth" and "two births" pertain to the final stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*);
thus, it is said that the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) and the position of the future Buddha (*upapadya-bodhisattva*) constitute "one birth," while the ninth stage constitutes "two births.

If one were to discuss this fully, it would be according to the meaning of "reducing births" (*sunsheng*) as taught in the *Lotus Sūtra*; such an explanation refers to the same principle as the "discriminative" [teaching].

In the "Chapter on Merit" (*Guṇa-pada*), the text states that one shall attain [the fruit] in a single lifetime (*ekajātipratibaddha*); yet, the present passage speaks of "breaking through one or two grades of ignorance" (*avidyā*).

This refers to the initial stage. There is no other reason for this: it is because the intent of the Sūtra is manifold, and the Patriarchs’ applications of it need not always conform to a single standard.

This is just as in the passage concerning the fourfold differences in the wisdom that contemplates causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-jñāna*), which the Great Master [Zhiyi] has addressed in many places.
In the "Section on Citation," [the text] addresses the four teachings; however, the commentary and the present text treat the "separate and combined" (*bie-jie-tong*) as distinct to explain them.

Could it be that Zhanran (Zhang’an) and Jingxi specifically contravened the Great Master? Therefore, we know that the meaning of the sutra is manifold, and its application follows the specific passage at hand.
Herein, in order to clarify the meaning of the entry into the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], it is judged to belong to the initial stage. This is evident within the text itself.
"The phrase 'the wisdom and understanding of An [Hui] differ' is a statement from the *Shu* (Commentary) regarding the sequence of "one giving rise to two.
The words "going on to record" (*qùjì*) are the terms used by the Master [Zhiyi] to deliberate and provide his own judgment and interpretation; the rest may be understood accordingly. Question:

In the *Miaoxuan*, the Great Master judges that the "Holy Practices" chapter (*Shengxing pin*) of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the sequential exposition (*zhuishuo*) of the four teachings, while the nineteenth chapter, "The Virtuous King" (*Dewang pin*), clarifies the sequential sublation (*zhumin*) of the four teachings. Since they are both sequential, why is there a distinction?"

Question: Since the Dharma Flower Sūtra (Lotus Sūtra) opens the assembly to reveal that the One Way is without partiality, why does the end of the sūtra further clarify the process of "being received" (*beijie*)?
Answer: The *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel) states: "In terms of the sections, it is said to apply to 'all'; within the various categories of the sections, there are both the real and the provisional.

Thus we know that the Great Master merely pointed to two specific chapters to demonstrate the characteristics of "subsequent teaching" (*zhuishuo*) and "subsequent sublation" (*zhumin*); in reality, these two meanings encompass everything.
The meaning of each sūtra is profound and subtle; were it not for the guidance of the Patriarchs, by what means could one come to know it?
When discussing the categories to which the śrāvakas belong, one must first investigate the origin from which they derive their name, and then [the classification] will naturally follow.

To organize these points without confusion: the reason this present sutra surpasses all other teachings of a single era is that it is able to open the way for those who are otherwise difficult to open.
When my Buddha-trace served as a prince and gave a comprehensive lecture, which of the śrāvakas did not plant the seeds of conditions for the Mahāyāna?
Those who received their predictions after the three cycles of teaching, as well as those who turned their minds toward enlightenment after my parinirvāṇa, are all [included therein].
This is so. Judging from this, it is entirely reasonable to say that although both are called "regressing from the Great" (*dà tuì*), the principle is indeed as stated.

However, if our Buddha had not recounted the events of the Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū Tathāgata, who would have known of this regression from the Great? Therefore, it is said: "Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, who would have known of the regression from the Great?
For this reason, from the period at the Deer Park onwards, the mind that clings to the Truth and preserves the Fruit has been the same for everyone.

It may also be appropriate to refer to all of them uniformly as those of "fixed nature" (niyata-gotra). Thus it is said: "Those on the stage of *samatā* and those on the same seat are all called 'extinguished seeds'.

However, because this teaching is explained as being provisional and discussed according to expedient means, it is necessary to present it in two stages. If that is so, should the other three teachings also be treated in this way?

Regarding the path of teaching (*śāstramārga*) as explained in terms of realization (*adhigama*), it pervades the beginning and end of a single teaching; therefore, even from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the path of teaching still persists.

If one speaks of the dharmas realized from the ten stages onward, these belong to the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*) alone. As for the other three [paths], they do not possess this quality and are thus not discussed here.

Furthermore, it is asked: regarding these four types, some claim that only the path of practice (*pratipattimārga*) and the path of realization belong to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), while the other three belong to...

[The interlocutor] asks: "Since both belong to the reality (*tattva*), why are they divided into two kinds? [The Master] answers:

This is explained in terms of the Path of Teaching. Sentient beings of distinct capacities rely on the teaching to practice:

The evidence for this is found in the teachings on the practitioner’s progress; thus, these are the scriptural proofs concerning the practice.

Nevertheless, regarding the exposition of the path of realization (*darśanamārga*), there is no separate dharma-gate; rather, it is simply a matter of pointing out the distinct stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*) to those whose wisdom has already been transformed, so that these may become perfectly integrated (*yuganaddha*).
This is because, although their wisdom has been transformed, such individuals must still rely upon the teachings to further break through [delusions].
If, due to ignorance, one must still rely on the teachings even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), how much more so should one doubt this [present teaching]?

It merely points out that the distinct (*li-bie*) dharmas heard at the time of the initial mind are themselves the perfect fusion. If that were so, then it would be named...

Furthermore, it is asked: Since it is said that pointing out the gradual and separate is itself the perfectly integrated (*yuanrong*), is this not the Perfect Teaching grafting onto the Separate Teaching? Answer: It is the Shared Teaching.
